# Second pass: evaluate cuts and revise

The original source, validated preservation plan, and first draft follow.
The first draft has been counted by code. Its numbered paragraphs include
their measured word counts and any protected passages they contain.

The single fixed target is 1000 words.
The first draft contains 1500 words.
The measured difference, first draft minus target, is 500 words.

Remove a net 500 words from the first draft.


Evaluate the available cuts before revising. Use the paragraph counts to choose
enough material to achieve the required net change. Prefer whole optional
sentences, exchanges, examples and repetitions. A long paragraph containing one
protected excerpt is not wholly protected. Essential functions may be expressed
more economically; they do not require every surrounding sentence.

Treat the first draft as text to edit, not as a synopsis to rewrite. Leave
surviving sentences unchanged unless a specific cut creates a connection that
needs repair or the source reveals an error. Preserve performed dialogue and
the author's sentence construction. Prefer a larger optional deletion to many
small paraphrases across otherwise sound passages.

For each significant candidate, record a brief editorial decision: cut,
compress, keep, or restore; identify its first-draft paragraph numbers; explain
the reason and the dependent setup, payoff, speaker, reference or argument that
must remain connected. Include important rejected cuts where they explain why
another passage was shortened. This is a concise editorial audit, not private
reasoning. The audit must describe the revision you actually return.

Preserve every required exact excerpt. Restore any missing protected excerpt
identified by code, using the original source. Preserve source uncertainty,
qualifications, comic timing, characteristic rhythms and period language.
Do not replace performed dialogue or argument with generic plot summary.
Keep speakers in separate paragraphs and retain source-supported attribution.
Do not import the later facts provided as cross-chapter evidence. Keep the
ending complete. Repair orphaned names, objects and callbacks after cuts.

Account for any added bridge or restored material in the net reduction.
Use the supplied measurements rather than assuming your estimate is accurate.
Your revised text will be counted again by code. Do not claim an exact count
that has not been measured. If the preservation requirements cannot fit, return
a complete best effort, set infeasible to true and explain the specific conflict.

Return only the complete revised chapter, without a title, followed by exactly
one final comment. Editorial notes do not count toward the chapter length.

His words woke a vague alarm in her. What if there\n_was_ some one concealed in the house? Some one who might bar that door\non them, and leave them to die like rats in a trap? Then she realized\nthe absurdity of her thought. The house was surrounded by police who,\nif they failed to reappear, would not hesitate to break in and make a\nthorough search. She smiled at her own foolishness--then looked up with\na start to find Sir James watching her. He gave her an emphatic little\nnod.\n\n“Quite right, Miss Tuppence. You scent danger. So do I. So does Miss\nFinn.”\n\n“Yes,” admitted Jane. “It’s absurd--but I can’t help it.”\n\nSir James nodded again.\n\n“You feel--as we all feel-- _the presence of Mr. Bown_. Yes”--as\nTuppence made a movement--“not a doubt of it-- _Mr. Brown is here_....”\n\n“In this house?”\n\n“In this room.... You don’t understand? _I am Mr. Brown_....”\n\nStupefied, unbelieving, they stared at him. The very lines of his face\nhad changed. It was a different man who stood before them. He smiled a\nslow cruel smile.\n\n“Neither of you will leave this room alive! You said just now we had\nsucceeded. _I_ have succeeded! The draft treaty is mine.” His smile grew\nwider as he looked at Tuppence. “Shall I tell you how it will be? Sooner\nor later the police will break in, and they will find three victims of\nMr. Brown--three, not two, you understand, but fortunately the third\nwill not be dead, only wounded, and will be able to describe the attack\nwith a wealth of detail! The treaty? It is in the hands of Mr. Brown. So\nno one will think of searching the pockets of Sir James Peel Edgerton!”\n\nHe turned to Jane.\n\n“You outwitted me. I make my acknowledgments. But you will not do it\nagain.”\n\nThere was a faint sound behind him, but, intoxicated with success, he\ndid not turn his head.\n\nHe slipped his hand into his pocket.\n\n“Checkmate to the Young Adventurers,” he said, and slowly raised the big\nautomatic.\n\nBut, even as he did so, he felt himself seized from behind in a grip of\niron. The revolver was wrenched from his hand, and the voice of Julius\nHersheimmer said drawlingly:\n\n“I guess you’re caught redhanded with the goods upon you.”\n\nThe blood rushed to the K.C.’s face, but his self-control was\nmarvellous, as he looked from one to the other of his two captors. He\nlooked longest at Tommy.\n\n“You,” he said beneath his breath. “_You!_ I might have known.”\n\nSeeing that he was disposed to offer no resistance, their grip\nslackened. Quick as a flash his left hand, the hand which bore the big\nsignet ring, was raised to his lips....\n\n“‘_Ave, Cæsar! te morituri salutant_,’” he said, still looking at\nTommy.\n\nThen his face changed, and with a long convulsive shudder he fell\nforward in a crumpled heap, whilst an odour of bitter almonds filled the\nair.\n"}
